claim: The structure and diversity of microbial communities are intrinsically hierarchical due to the shared evolutionary history of their constituents.
source: The structure and diversity of microbial communities are intrinsically hierarchical due to the shared evolutionary history of their constituents.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of microbial communities based on established understanding of evolutionary relationships.

claim: A single environmental sample typically has a high richness, harboring hundreds to thousands of community members.
source: A single environmental sample typically has a high richness, harboring hundreds to thousands of community members (Thompson et al., 2017; Shoemaker et al., 2017; Barberán et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Scaling relationships and models of biodiversity predict upwards of one trillion (∼10^12) species on Earth.
source: This high level of richness reaches an astronomical quantity at the global level, as scaling relationships and models of biodiversity predict upwards of one trillion (∼1012) species on Earth (Locey and Lennon, 2016; Lennon and Locey, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Experimental communities in laboratory settings with a single carbon source can harbor ≥40 community members.
source: Even experimental communities in laboratory settings with a single carbon source can harbor ≥40 community members, culminating in a total richness numbering in the hundreds among replicate communities (e.g. Dal Bello et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The choice of assigning a community member to a given taxon remains intrinsically arbitrary.
source: While richness estimates of microbial communities are undoubtedly high, the choice of assigning a community member to a given taxon remains intrinsically arbitrary.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the nature of taxonomic assignment.

claim: Microbial richness/diversity within a given taxonomic group is typically positively correlated with the richness/diversity among the remaining groups.
source: Specifically, recent efforts have found that microbial richness/diversity within a given taxonomic group (e.g. genus) is typically positively correlated with the richness/diversity among the remaining groups (e.g. family) (Madi et al., 2020; Estrela et al., 2022), an empirical pattern that aligns with the predictions of the Diversity Begets Diversity (DBD) hypothesis (Whittaker, 1972; San Roman et al., 2018; Maynard et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Evidence of the DBD hypothesis has historically been attributed to the construction of novel niches within a community through member interactions.
source: Evidence of the DBD hypothesis has historically been attributed to the construction of novel niches within a community through member interactions (Calcagno et al., 2017; Whittaker, 1972), with similar mechanisms having been proposed to explain the existence of a positive relationship in microbial communities (Madi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The UNTB generally fails to capture basic patterns of microbial diversity and abundance at any scale.
source: By this standard, the UNTB is an unsuitable choice as a null as it generally fails to capture basic patterns of microbial diversity and abundance at any scale (Li and Ma, 2016; Harris et al., 2017; Grilli, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The UNTB predicts that the distribution of mean abundances of community members across sites is extremely narrow, whereas empirical data tends to follow a broad lognormal distribution.
source: One relevant example is that the UNTB predicts that the distribution of mean abundances of community members across sites is extremely narrow (i.e. converging to a delta distribution as the number of sites increases), whereas empirical data tends to follow a broad lognormal distribution (Grilli, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The SLM is capable of quantitatively capturing multiple empirical macroecological patterns in observational and experimental microbial communities.
source: Contrastingly, recent efforts have determined that the predictions of a model of self-limiting growth with environmental noise, the SLM, is capable of quantitatively capturing multiple empirical macroecological patterns in observational and experimental microbial communities (Grilli, 2020; Zaoli and Grilli, 2021; Zaoli et al., 2022; Descheemaeker et al., 2021; Descheemaeker and de Buyl, 2020; Shoemaker et al., 2023c; Lim et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The stationary solution of the SLM predicts that the abundance of a given community member across sites follows a gamma distribution.
source: The stationary solution of this model predicts that the abundance of a given community member across sites follows a gamma distribution (Grilli, 2020), a result that provides the foundation necessary to predict macroecological patterns among and between different taxonomic and phylogenetic scales.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Even minor degrees of coarse-graining had a drastic effect on the total number of community members within an environment, reducing global richness by ∼90% even at just the genus level.
source: We found that even minor degrees of coarse-graining had a drastic effect on the total number of community members within an environment, reducing global richness by ∼90% even at just the genus level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in a figure.

claim: The fraction of coarse-grained community members comparable to that of genus-level coarse-graining occurred at a root-to-tip phylogenetic distance of ∼0.1.
source: By coarse-graining over a range of phylogenetic distances, we found that the fraction of coarse-grained community members comparable to that of genus-level coarse-graining occurred at a root-to-tip phylogenetic distance of ∼0.1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in a figure.

claim: AFDs from the human gut microbiome retained their shape across phylogenetic scales.
source: By coarse-graining empirical AFDs and rescaling them by their mean and variance across sites (i.e. standard score), we found that AFDs from the human gut microbiome retained their shape across phylogenetic scales (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in a figure.

claim: Empirical AFDs can likely be described by a single probability distribution across phylogenetic and taxonomic scales.
source: This pattern of invariance held across environments for both phylogenetic and taxonomic coarse-graining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that empirical AFDs can likely be described by a single probability distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Equation 1 generally succeeded in predicting observed occupancy across phylogenetic and taxonomic scales for all environments.
source: We found that Equation 1 generally succeeded in predicting observed occupancy across phylogenetic and taxonomic scales for all environments (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: The gamma distribution is capable of capturing the relationship between the mean abundance and occupancy across taxonomic and phylogenetic scales for all environments.
source: We see that this relationship is broadly captured across taxonomic and phylogenetic scales for all environments (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: The gamma distribution was unable to predict the variance of occupancy under both taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining.
source: In contrast with these results, the gamma distribution was unable to predict the variance of occupancy under both taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining (Equation 11; Figure 2—figure supplement 7, Figure 2—figure supplement 8), the implications of which we will address in a later section.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: The mean logarithm of the error of mean occupancy predictions only slightly increased for the initial taxonomic and phylogenetic scales, where it then exhibited a sharp decrease across environments.
source: We found that the mean logarithm of the error only slightly increased for the initial taxonomic and phylogenetic scales, where it then exhibited a sharp decrease across environments (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in a figure.

claim: The strongest correlations between AFDs are typically concentrated among pairs of closely related community members.
source: These results are consistent with previous efforts demonstrating that the strongest correlations between AFDs are typically concentrated among pairs of closely related community members (i.e. low phylogenetic distance) (Sireci et al., 2023), implying that the effects of correlation should dissipate when communities are coarse-grained.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A single gamma distribution can provide a suitable approximation to the distribution of the sum of many gamma random variables with different rate parameters.
source: This body of work includes an analysis demonstrating that a single gamma distribution can provide a suitable approximation to the distribution of the sum of many gamma random variables with different rate parameters (Covo and Elalouf, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The gamma distribution appears to successfully capture patterns of biodiversity under taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining because the sum of multiple gamma distributions can be approximated by a single gamma distribution.
source: In summary, the gamma distribution appears to successfully captures patterns of biodiversity under taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining because the sum of multiple gamma distributions can be approximated by a single gamma distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis and cited literature.

claim: The gamma distribution is capable of predicting the typical richness of a community across phylogenetic scales.
source: Focusing on the human gut microbiome as an example, we found that we can predict the typical richness of a community across phylogenetic scales using the gamma distribution (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in a figure.

claim: The gamma distribution is capable of predicting mean diversity across phylogenetic scales.
source: Similar results were obtained when we repeated our analysis for predicted diversity (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in a figure.

claim: Despite the dissimilarity in environments, the gamma distribution was able to predict mean richness and diversity in the face of coarse-graining across all nine environments.
source: By examining all nine environments we found that despite the dissimilarity in environments, we were able to predict mean richness and diversity in the face of coarse-graining (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: The UNTB failed to predict richness.
source: In contrast, the UNTB failed to predict richness (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in a figure.

claim: The composition of microbial communities remained largely invariant under coarse-graining.
source: The results of this analysis suggest that the composition of microbial communities remained largely invariant under coarse-graining and that the gamma distribution remained a suitable null model for predicting mean community measures across coarse-grained scales.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of richness and diversity predictions.

claim: Analytic predictions typically fail to capture estimates of variance of richness obtained from empirical data for phylogenetic coarse-graining.
source: With the human gut as an example, we see that analytic predictions typically fail to capture estimates of variance obtained from empirical data for phylogenetic coarse-graining (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: A model of independent community members with gamma-distributed abundances was insufficient to capture the variance of measures of biodiversity.
source: This lack of predictive success was consistent across environments (Figure 4c and d), implying that a model of independent community members with gamma-distributed abundances was insufficient to capture the variance of measures of biodiversity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures and represents an inference from the data.

claim: The addition of empirical estimates of covariance was sufficient to predict the observed variance of richness and diversity.
source: We found that the addition of this empirical estimate was sufficient to predict the observed variance in the human gut (Figure 4a and b) as well as across environments (Figure 4e and f), implying that the underlying model is fundamentally correct for predicting the first moment of measures of biodiversity but cannot capture the correlations necessary to explain higher statistical moments such as the variance.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: The distribution of empirical slopes pooled over all coarse-graining thresholds for each environment were rarely less than zero.
source: By examining the distribution of empirical slopes pooled over all coarse-graining thresholds for each environment, we found that they were rarely less than zero (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: The few negative slopes inferred from empirical data were extremely small, having absolute values <10^-4 and could be treated as zeros.
source: The few negative slopes inferred from empirical data were extremely small, having absolute values <10−4 and could be treated as zeros.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The distribution of slopes follows the same form across environments, suggesting that the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship reflects a general feature of community sequence data rather than the ecology of specific environments.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of slopes follows the same form across environments, suggesting that the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship reflects a general feature of community sequence data rather than the ecology of specific environments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that slope distributions are similar across environments.

claim: The gamma distribution virtually always predicted a positive slope for all environments for both taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining.
source: Like the empirical slopes, the gamma distribution virtually always predicted a positive slope for all environments for both taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining.
evidence: This is an observation from the model predictions.

claim: The prediction of the alternative to the DBD hypothesis, the Ecological Controls hypothesis, is virtually absent in empirical data and cannot be generated from an empirically validated null model of microbial biodiversity.
source: This paucity of negative slopes suggests that the prediction of the alternative to the DBD hypothesis, the Ecological Controls hypothesis (Schluter and Pennell, 2017), is virtually absent in empirical data and cannot be generated from an empirically validated null model of microbial biodiversity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that negative slopes are rare in both data and model predictions.

claim: The predictions of the gamma distribution closely matched the observed slopes of the fine vs. coarse-grained richness relationship across environments for both taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining.
source: We found that the predictions of the gamma distribution closely matched the observed slopes across environments for both taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: The mean slope predicted by the gamma distribution does a reasonable job capturing empirical slopes across environments.
source: We consolidated these results by taking the mean slope for a given coarse-grained scale, from which we see that the mean slope predicted by the gamma distribution does a reasonable job capturing empirical slopes across environments (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: We should expect to see a positive relationship between richness estimates at different scales and that the relationships we observe can be quantitatively captured by a gamma-distributed AFD.
source: These results indicate that we should expect to see a positive relationship between richness estimates at different scales and that the relationships we observe can be quantitatively captured by a gamma-distributed AFD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of fine vs. coarse-grained richness slopes.

claim: Higher-order statistical moments, and by extension interactions between community members, are unnecessary to quantitatively capture the positive relationship observed between fine and coarse-grained estimates of richness.
source: It is worth noting that the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship could be sufficiently predicted even though the gamma distribution only succeeded at predicting mean richness, suggesting that higher-order statistical moments, and by extension interactions between community members, are unnecessary to quantitatively capture the positive relationship observed between fine and coarse-grained estimates of richness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that richness slopes can be predicted without predicting variance.

claim: The UNTB slopes deviated from those obtained from empirical data, exhibiting far greater bias and variation around the 1:1 line than what was observed of the SLM.
source: We found that generally, the UNTB slopes deviated from those obtained from empirical data, exhibiting far greater bias and variation around the 1:1 line than what was observed of the SLM (Figure 5—figure supplement 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: Predictions from the UNTB tended to systematically underpredict the observed slope under both taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining.
source: By examining the mean slope we found that predictions from the UNTB tended to systematically underpredict the observed slope under both taxonomic and phylogenetic coarse-graining (Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in a figure.

claim: The UNTB predictions tended to have larger errors by an order of magnitude compared to the SLM.
source: Directly comparing the mean relative error of the UNTB predictions to those of the SLM confirms these observations, as the UNTB predictions tended to have larger errors by an order of magnitude (Figure 5—figure supplement 8, Figure 5—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: In contrast to the SLM, the UNTB cannot predict the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship for richness.
source: To summarize, in contrast to the SLM, the UNTB cannot predict the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship for richness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of SLM and UNTB predictions.

claim: Disparate environments had similar distributions of slopes from empirical data for diversity.
source: We again found that disparate environments had similar distributions of slopes from empirical data (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 2c), suggesting that the slope of the relationship is likely a general property of microbial communities rather than an environment-specific pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: Diversity predictions obtained from the gamma distribution generally failed to capture observed slopes.
source: However, unlike richness, diversity predictions obtained from the gamma distribution generally failed to capture observed slopes, as the squared correlation between observed and predicted slopes can be less than that of richness by over an order of magnitude (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 10, Figure 5—figure supplement 11, Figure 5—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: By including correlations between AFDs into the simulations, we were able to largely capture observed fine vs. coarse-grained diversity slopes.
source: By including correlations between AFDs into the simulations, the statistical outcome of ecological interactions between community members, we were able to largely capture observed fine vs. coarse-grained diversity slopes (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in figures.

claim: Rather than diversity at a fine-scale begetting diversity at a coarse-scale, the correlations that exist at a fine-scale contribute to measures of biodiversity at the nearest coarse-grained scale, resulting in a positive relationship between measures of diversity at different scales.
source: These results suggest that rather than diversity at a fine-scale begetting diversity at a coarse-scale, the correlations that exist at a fine-scale (e.g. genus) contribute to measures of biodiversity at the nearest coarse-grained scale (e.g. family), resulting in a positive relationship between measures of diversity at different scales.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results showing that correlations are necessary to predict diversity slopes.

claim: Macroecological patterns in microbial communities remain largely invariant across taxonomic and phylogenetic scales.
source: The results of this study demonstrate that macroecological patterns in microbial communities remain largely invariant across taxonomic and phylogenetic scales.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the results of the study.

claim: Certain macroecological patterns of microbial communities remained self-similar across taxonomic and phylogenetic scales.
source: We were largely able to predict said measures using the same model with parameters estimated from data across scales, implying that certain macroecological patterns of microbial communities remained self-similar across taxonomic and phylogenetic scales.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ability to predict measures of biodiversity across scales.

claim: The prediction derived from the sampling form of the gamma distribution quantitatively captured the observed slopes of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship for richness.
source: The prediction derived from the sampling form of the gamma distribution quantitatively captured the observed slopes of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship for richness, while it failed to capture the slope of diversity.
evidence: This is a summary of the results for richness and diversity slopes.

claim: Introducing correlations between abundance fluctuation distribution permitted the recovery of the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained diversity relationship.
source: However, introducing correlations between abundance fluctuation distribution permitted the recovery of the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained diversity relationship.
evidence: This is a summary of the simulation results for diversity slopes.

claim: Occupancy is highly dependent on two parameters: sampling depth and the mean abundance of a community member.
source: Our richness results complement past work demonstrating that occupancy, the constituent of richness, is highly dependent on two parameters: sampling depth (i.e. total read count) and the mean abundance of a community member (Grilli, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Occupancy alone is unlikely to contain ecological information that is not already captured by the distribution of abundances across sites.
source: This past work, and the relationships between the mean abundance and occupancy evaluated in this manuscript, demonstrate that occupancy alone is unlikely to contain ecological information that is not already captured by the distribution of abundances across sites (i.e. the AFD).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results and prior research.

claim: The success of an interaction-free model in predicting the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship is an indictment of the appropriateness of estimators that rely solely on the presence of a community member for identifying novel macroecological patterns.
source: The success of an interaction-free model in predicting the slope of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship is an indictment of the appropriateness of estimators that rely solely on the presence of a community member for identifying novel macroecological patterns, a measure that has been used to bolster support for the DBD hypothesis at the level of 16S rRNA amplicons as well as strains (Madi et al., 2020; Madi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results and represents a critique of prior work.

claim: Estimates of richness harbor little information about the dynamics of a community across taxonomic and phylogenetic scales that is not already captured by the sampling form of the gamma distribution.
source: Rather, estimates of richness harbor little information about the dynamics of a community across taxonomic and phylogenetic scales that is not already captured by the sampling form of the gamma distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of richness predictions.

claim: Forms of the SLM that neglect interactions between community members cannot capture relationships between phylogenetic/taxonomic scales that depend on the evenness of the distribution of abundances.
source: Given that measures of diversity incorporate information about the richness and evenness of a community (Magurran, 2004), the comparative deficiency of our predictions for fine vs. coarse-grained diversity suggests that forms of the SLM that neglect interactions between community members cannot capture relationships between phylogenetic/taxonomic scales that depend on the evenness of the distribution of abundances.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the failure to predict diversity slopes without correlations.

claim: The novelty of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship was previously assessed using a null model which assumed demographic equivalence among community members and community dynamics driven by demographic noise.
source: The novelty of the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship was previously assessed using a null model which assumed demographic equivalence among community members and community dynamics driven by demographic noise (i.e. the UNTB) (Madi et al., 2020; Alonso and McKane, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Empirical patterns of microbial abundance cannot be reasonably captured by the UNTB, making predictions obtained from the UNTB invalid for evaluating the novelty of microbial macroecological patterns.
source: Empirical patterns of microbial abundance cannot be reasonably captured by such models, making predictions obtained from the UNTB invalid for evaluating the novelty of microbial macroecological patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of UNTB predictions to empirical data.

claim: Models that combine self-limiting growth with environmental noise reproduce several empirical patterns, making the SLM an appropriate choice for evaluating the novelty of fine vs. coarse-grained relationships.
source: In contrast, models that combine self-limiting growth with environmental noise reproduces several empirical patterns, making the SLM an appropriate choice for evaluating the novelty of fine vs. coarse-grained relationships (Grilli, 2020; Descheemaeker and de Buyl, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Any ecological mechanism that can capture the observed distribution of correlation coefficients is a plausible candidate for explaining the fine vs. coarse-grained diversity relationship.
source: This result suggests that rather than exclusively pointing to niche construction as previously suggested (Madi et al., 2020), any ecological mechanism that can capture the observed distribution of correlation coefficients is a plausible candidate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results showing that correlations are necessary to predict diversity slopes.

claim: Models of consumer-resource dynamics have succeeded in capturing macroecological patterns, including quantitatively predicting the distribution of correlation coefficients.
source: Given that models of consumer-resource dynamics have succeeded in capturing macroecological patterns (Chesson, 1990; Cui et al., 2021), including quantitatively predicting the distribution of correlation coefficients (Ho et al., 2022), it is reasonable to suggest that such mechanisms are ultimately responsible for the relationship between fine and coarse-grained measures of diversity and can be reduced to phenomenological models such as the SLM.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Experimental investigations of the slopes evaluated here have found the existence of positive slopes in artificial communities maintained in a laboratory setting, where the strength of the correlation between fine and coarse-grained scales is driven by the secretion of secondary metabolites.
source: Indeed, experimental investigations of the slopes evaluated here have found the existence of positive slopes in artificial communities maintained in a laboratory setting, where the strength of the correlation between fine and coarse-grained scales is driven by the secretion of secondary metabolites (Estrela et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cross-feeding can be viewed as compatible with the concept of niche construction as well as with the original interpretation of Madi et al., 2020.
source: This mechanism, known as cross-feeding, can be viewed as compatible with the concept of niche construction (San Roman et al., 2018) as well as with the original interpretation of Madi et al., 2020.
evidence: This is an inference about the compatibility of different interpretations.

claim: The AFD correlation between two community members is often inversely related to their phylogenetic distance.
source: However, given that the AFD correlation between two community members is often inversely related to their phylogenetic distance, such an analysis would likely be redundant, as coarse-graining based on the strength of correlation would effectively coarse-grain the most closely related community members (Sireci et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The stationary solution of the SLM has successfully characterized microbial community time-series at both the level of OTUs and strains.
source: This assumption can remain valid for time-series studies where the distribution of microbial abundances remains stationary with respect to time (Faith et al., 2013), as the stationary solution of the SLM has successfully characterized microbial community time-series at both the level of OTUs (Grilli, 2020) and strains (Wolff et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The fine vs. coarse-grained relationship results presented here will remain valid in longitudinal studies where community members fluctuate around a single point with respect to time.
source: Given these past results, we predict that the fine vs. coarse-grained relationship results presented here will remain valid in longitudinal studies where community members fluctuate around a single point with respect to time.
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior research and the results of this study.

claim: Data was downloaded from the Earth Microbiome Project.
source: To ensure that our analyses were generalizable across ecosystems and commensurate with prior DBD investigations, we used amplicon sequence data from the V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene generated and curated by the Earth Microbiome Project (Thompson et al., 2017; Madi et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: The analysis was restricted to the quality control (QC)-filtered subset of the EMP, which was annotated using the closed-reference database SILVA.
source: We restricted our analysis to the quality control (QC)-filtered subset of the EMP, which was annotated using the closed-reference database SILVA (Quast et al., 2013) and consists of 96 studies culminating in 23,828 total samples with each processed sample having ≥10,000 reads.
evidence: This describes the data processing and filtering steps.

claim: Nine heavily sampled environments were identified in the metadata file and 100 random sites were selected from each environment.
source: We identified nine heavily sampled environments in the metadata file emp_qiime_mapping_qc_filtered.tsv and selected 100 random sites from each environment.
evidence: This describes the sampling strategy used in the study.

claim: Taxonomic coarse-graining was performed as the summation of the abundances of all OTUs within a given taxonomic group.
source: Taxonomic coarse-graining was performed as the summation of the abundances of all OTUs within a given taxonomic group.
evidence: This describes the method used for taxonomic coarse-graining.

claim: Taxa with indeterminate labels were removed to prevent potential biases due to taxonomic misassignment.
source: We removed taxa with indeterminate labels to prevent potential biases due to taxonomic misassignment, (e.g. 'uncultured,' 'ambiguous taxa,' 'candidatus,' 'unclassified,' etc.).
evidence: This describes a data cleaning step.

claim: Phylogenetic coarse-graining was performed using the phylogenetic tree provided by SILVA 123 97_otus.tre in the EMP release.
source: Phylogenetic coarse-graining was performed using the phylogenetic tree provided by SILVA 123 97_otus.tre in the EMP release.
evidence: This describes the method used for phylogenetic coarse-graining.

claim: Each internal node of a phylogenetic tree was collapsed if the mean branch lengths of its descendants was less than a given distance.
source: Each internal node of a phylogenetic tree was collapsed if the mean branch lengths of its descendants was less than a given distance.
evidence: This describes the method used for phylogenetic coarse-graining.

claim: The stationary distribution of the SLM can be derived using the Itô ↔ Fokker-Planck equivalence and solving for the stationary solution, resulting in the gamma-distributed AFD.
source: The stationary distribution of the SLM can be derived using the Itô ↔ Fokker-Planck equivalence and solving for the stationary solution (Grilli, 2020; Engen and Lande, 1996), resulting in the gamma-distributed AFD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Correlated gamma-distributed AFDs were simulated by performing inverse transform sampling.
source: Correlated gamma-distributed AFDs were simulated by performing inverse transform sampling.
evidence: This describes the simulation method used.
